verdict:
This is an IP-level block of <old-ip> enforced across Russia. It is not specific to one ISP or one region, and it does not cover the whole subnet or the whole hoster. Confidence that it is Russia-wide and per-IP: high.

How the evidence fits together:
(1) The same single IP is dropped from unrelated ISPs in different regions. Home lines: Rostelecom Nizhny Novgorod and Kostroma, MTS Novosibirsk x2, Vimpelcom Ufa, NCN Moscow. Ural: Izet Telecom Yekaterinburg and GalaxyStar Nizhny Tagil (upstream ER-Telecom). About 35 of 40 RU datacenter networks drop it too. This matches the owner's own Rostelecom Yekaterinburg test. Every one of these probes is healthy: 1.1.1.1 answers at 0% loss.
(2) The neighbor <old-net>.150 in the same /24 is reachable from all of the same probes at the same time: TCP 443 40/40 + 20/20 + 7/7 + 2/2, ICMP 20/20 + 7/7 + 2/2. A further 14 of 16 live neighbors are reachable from the Moscow check-host nodes. So the block is not on the subnet, the hoster (AS213877 u1host) or the transit path, and foreign traffic in general is not blocked.
(3) Traceroutes to .107 stop at the first or second hop inside each access ISP. Traceroutes to .150 cross the same Rostelecom / ER-Telecom backbone to AS49418 and finish. So the drop happens at the ISP edge, where RKN's TSPU filters sit, on a list pushed to every ISP. It is not a BGP problem: the route is visible in Moscow via AS12389. The IP is also not in the public RKN registry.
(4) Outside Russia the server is reachable everywhere: NL, DE, PL, KZ, BY, TR, US all 0% loss.

Is this a mass wave ('вышел пост')? The mechanism is a targeted per-IP listing, not a blanket ban on foreign hosting. But it is probably part of a wider sweep of VPN endpoints. A second IP in the same /24 (.100, another u1host VM) is blocked exactly the same way. The friend's separate server broke the same day. And coverage grew while I was measuring: Selectel SPb, GIS Novosibirsk and Khabarovsk could still connect at 20:08 UTC but not at 21:09 UTC. Confidence that it belongs to a wider wave: medium. Measurements cannot prove the date the IP was listed or the cause; the colleague angle cannot be excluded either.

The block is not complete everywhere yet. check-host ru3 (St Petersburg, AS210644) connected on every port in both rounds, and TIME-HOST Moscow, Vimpelcom Moscow (2/3) and Adman Novosibirsk (2/3) mostly got through. That fits the Planeta (AS31499) SSTP session still being alive: either Planeta's filter has not picked the IP up yet, or the flow was established before the block. There are no Globalping probes in AS31499, ER-Telecom, MegaFon or the Nizhny Tagil eyeball ISPs, so I could not test Planeta directly.

ICMP behaves differently by network. Home ISPs drop ICMP as well. Many datacenter paths, including both Moscow check-host nodes, let ICMP through and drop TCP.

Caveats: the server's own port state changed during the run (at ~20:35-20:50 UTC, 443 was refused and 8443/2053 toggled), so the 8443 data from after 20:35 is unusable. The 443/22 results are paired with simultaneous non-RU successes and are valid. The two control servers 72.4.71.232 and 185.121.12.185 were unreachable from everywhere, so they could not be used. The UDP check and ping-admin.ru gave no usable data.

Practical consequence: a new IP from the same hoster, or even from the same /24, should work until it is detected and listed. Moving the endpoint fixes it; nothing on the server needs fixing.
